The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. A compact smooth manifold $M$, possibly with boundary, has a finite relatively open good cover refining any specified open cover. Its nonempty finite intersections are contractible, with contractions depending smoothly on the endpoint and contraction parameter. The cover can be chosen with a smooth subordinate partition of unity whose supports lie in their assigned cover members. For its finite nerve $N$, there is a homotopy equivalence $M\to |N|$, and simplicial nerve cohomology identifies with singular cohomology of $M$ with coefficients in any abelian group. These identifications commute with coefficient homomorphisms, in particular reduction $\mathbb Z\to\mathbb F_2$.

Assume AC. Let $B$ be a compact oriented smooth four-manifold, possibly with boundary. Every $x\in H_2(B;\mathbb Z)$ is represented by a closed oriented smooth embedded surface $i:F\hookrightarrow\operatorname{Int}B$, with disconnected or empty $F$ allowed. For its oriented normal plane bundle $\nu_F$,
$$\langle w_2(TB),\rho_2x\rangle=\langle e(\nu_F),[F]\rangle\pmod2.$$
If $x$ is torsion, this integer normal Euler number is zero. In particular $w_2(TB)$ evaluates to zero on the reductions of all integral torsion degree-two classes.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $R$ be a PID, $C$ a chain complex of free
$R$-modules, and $G$ an $R$-module. Then naturally
$$0\to\operatorname{Ext}^1_R(H_{n-1}C,G)\to H^n\operatorname{Hom}_R(C,G)\xrightarrow{\operatorname{ev}_n}\operatorname{Hom}_R(H_nC,G)\to0$$
is exact.

Assume AC. Let $M$ be a compact oriented smooth four-manifold, possibly with boundary, with a Riemannian metric. Its oriented tangent frame bundle admits a Spin$^c(4)$ lift if and only if $w_2(TM)$ is the reduction of some class in $H^2(M;\mathbb Z)$. The criterion includes torsion classes. It asserts existence, not a bijection between Spin$^c$ structures and integral lifts of $w_2$.

derivations.claim: By [F1], $B$ has the homotopy type of a finite simplicial complex. Its integral chain groups are finite free abelian groups. Finite integer row and column operations, using the Euclidean algorithm, give Smith forms for their boundary maps, so each integral homology group is finitely generated. Tensoring these finite matrices with $\mathbb Q$ kills exactly their finite cyclic factors and preserves their free ranks. The assumed vanishing of positive rational homology therefore makes both $H_1(B;\mathbb Z)$ and $H_2(B;\mathbb Z)$ finite torsion groups. No assertion about a choice of infinitely many generators is needed.

Every $x\in H_2(B;\mathbb Z)$ is torsion by step 1.1. Apply [F2]: its embedded oriented surface has integer normal Euler number zero. Hence $\langle w_2(TB),\rho_2x\rangle=0$. Thus the evaluation homomorphism of [F3] with $G=\mathbb F_2$ sends $w_2(TB)$ to zero on the entire integral group $H_2(B;\mathbb Z)$. By exactness, $w_2(TB)$ is the image of a class $v\in\operatorname{Ext}^1(H_1(B;\mathbb Z),\mathbb F_2)$. This also covers zero $H_2$, without requiring mod-two $H_2$ to vanish.

**The coefficient lift is onto, including two-torsion.** Write the finite group $H_1(B;\mathbb Z)$ as a finite direct sum of cyclic groups $\mathbb Z/n$. From the free resolution $0\to\mathbb Z\xrightarrow{n}\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z/n\to0$, applying $\operatorname{Hom}(-,G)$ gives $\operatorname{Ext}^1(\mathbb Z/n,G)=G/nG$. The coefficient reduction therefore induces the explicit map $\mathbb Z/n\to\mathbb F_2/n\mathbb F_2$. If $n$ is odd its target is zero; if $n$ is even its target is $\mathbb F_2$ and the reduction is onto. Finite direct sums give a surjection $\operatorname{Ext}^1(H_1(B),\mathbb Z)\to\operatorname{Ext}^1(H_1(B),\mathbb F_2)$. When $H_1=0$, both groups are zero and the same conclusion holds. Choose a preimage $\widetilde v$ of the one class $v$ in step 2.1.

Let $c\in H^2(B;\mathbb Z)$ be the image of $\widetilde v$ under the integral UCT injection. Naturality of [F3] under $\mathbb Z\to\mathbb F_2$ identifies its reduction with the mod-two UCT image of $v$, which is exactly $w_2(TB)$ by step 2.1. Thus $c$ is an actual integral lift. In fact it lies in the finite Ext subgroup; no assertion that distinct such lifts label distinct Spin$^c$ structures is made.

Choose a smooth Riemannian metric by a finite trivializing atlas and a smooth partition, as in the construction of [F1]. Apply [F4] to $B$ with this metric and the integral lift $c$. Its transition-cocycle construction produces the required Spin$^c(4)$ principal bundle and its equivariant map to the oriented tangent frame bundle. This proves the original existence claim. All possible finite cyclic two-primary factors were retained in step 3.1; neither a vanishing mod-two homology assumption nor a determinant-class bijection was used.

Let V→X be an oriented Euclidean real vector bundle of rank n, with oriented frame bundle P_SO(V). Use Spin(n)=Spin_N=1(ℝⁿ,−‖·‖²), the norm-one even subgroup of the negative-square Clifford algebra, and its standard twisted-Clifford homomorphism λ_n:Spin(n)→SO(n). A Spin structure on V is a principal Spin(n)-bundle P with a Spin(n)-equivariant two-fold map $\widetilde\lambda:P\to P_{SO}(V)$ covering the identity on X and satisfying $\widetilde\lambda(pg)=\widetilde\lambda(p)\lambda_n(g)$. Put $\operatorname{Spin}^c(n)=(\operatorname{Spin}(n)\times U(1))/\langle(-1,-1)\rangle$ and define $\lambda_n^c:\operatorname{Spin}^c(n)\to SO(n)$ by $\lambda_n^c([s,z])=\lambda_n(s)$. A Spin$^c$ structure is a principal Spin$^c(n)$-bundle $P_c$ with a $\operatorname{Spin}^c(n)$-equivariant map $\widetilde\lambda_c:P_c\to P_{SO}(V)$ over the identity satisfying $\widetilde\lambda_c(p g)=\widetilde\lambda_c(p)\lambda_n^c(g)$. A spinor bundle is the associated bundle for the specified real Clifford representation; a Spin$^c$ spinor bundle is $P_c\times_{\tau^c}S$, where the specified complex representation $\tau$ of $\operatorname{Spin}(n)$ and integer $U(1)$ weight $k$ satisfy $\tau(-1)(-1)^k=I_S$, and $\tau^c([s,z])=z^k\tau(s)$. This condition is exactly that $(-1,-1)$ act trivially, so the representation descends to the quotient. For the complex Clifford spinor representation, $\tau(-1)=-I_S$ and the standard weight is $k=1$. These are given structures; this definition asserts no existence criterion.

Let $G$ be a topological group, as in [[def-topological-group]], with identity $1$. A **right principal $G$-bundle** is a continuous map $\pi:P\to B$ with a continuous right action $(p,g)\mapsto pg$, satisfying $p1=p$, $(pg)h=p(gh)$ and $\pi(pg)=\pi(p)$, together with equivariant bundle charts $\theta_i:\pi^{-1}(U_i)\cong U_i\times G$ over an open cover. Equivariance means $\theta_i(pg)=(b,ag)$ whenever $\theta_i(p)=(b,a)$. Charts use ordinary products as in [[def-locally-trivial-fiber-bundle]]. In each fiber the action is free and transitive: right multiplication on $G$ has those properties and the chart identifies the actions. Freeness alone is not the definition.

A **left $G$-space** is a topological space $F$ with a continuous map $(g,x)\mapsto gx$ such that $1x=x$ and $g(hx)=(gh)x$. Effectiveness of this action is not required. Define
$$P\times_G F=(P\times F)/\bigl((pg,x)\sim(p,gx)\bigr)$$
with the ordinary quotient topology, and write $[p,x]$ for its points. Precisely, the relation is the orbit relation of the right action $(p,x)\cdot g=(pg,g^{-1}x)$. Its action law is $((p,x)\cdot g)\cdot h=(pgh,h^{-1}g^{-1}x)=(p,x)\cdot(gh)$, and its generating relations are exactly the displayed ones. Thus the equivalence relation and quotient are defined without choosing orbit representatives.

The projection $r([p,x])=\pi(p)$ is well-defined and continuous by [[thm-quotient-universal-property]], since $(p,x)\mapsto\pi(p)$ is continuous and constant on every orbit. This is the **associated fiber-bundle construction**; the next proposition proves its local triviality and pullback property. The quotient construction and projection already make sense before that proof.

If $B$ is empty then $P$ is empty. If $F$ is empty the associated space is empty even for nonempty $B$; this is allowed by our bundle convention. For singleton $F$ the construction is the orbit projection of the principal bundle. For the trivial group it is the product with $F$ over the chart-identified base. No AC is used.

For an ordinary right principal $G$-bundle $\pi:P\to B$ and a continuous left $G$-space $F$, the associated projection $r:P\times_G F\to B$ is a locally trivial bundle with fiber $F$. For every continuous $h:A\to B$ there is a canonical bundle isomorphism
$$\Phi:(h^*P)\times_G F\longrightarrow h^*(P\times_G F),\qquad \Phi([(a,p),x])=(a,[p,x]).$$
It respects identity and successive pullbacks. Neither AC nor effectiveness of the action on $F$ is required. All products, subspaces and quotients here are ordinary topological ones, as specified in the definition.

Assume AC. For a path-connected CW complex $X$ with a vertex basepoint, the
first Chern class induces a natural group isomorphism
$$c_1:\operatorname{Pic}_{\mathrm{top}}(X)\xrightarrow{\ \cong\ }H^2(X;\mathbb Z),$$
where $\operatorname{Pic}_{\mathrm{top}}(X)$ is the group of isomorphism
classes of numerable complex line bundles under tensor product. The same
statement holds for a path-connected paracompact Hausdorff CGWH space of CW
homotopy type.

derivations.claim: For any second lift $P_1$, define $L(P_0,P_1)_x$ to be the set of Spin$^c$-equivariant maps from $(P_0)_x$ to $(P_1)_x$ covering the identity map of the common oriented frame fiber. Since both are lifts of that same frame fiber, two such maps differ by a unique element of the central kernel $U(1)$ from [F1]. In local lift trivializations, the transition functions of $P_0$ and $P_1$ project to the same $\mathrm{SO}(n)$ functions, so their pointwise quotient lies in central $U(1)$; the cocycle identity for each lift makes these quotients a $U(1)$-valued cocycle. Thus the difference fibers form a principal $U(1)$-bundle $L(P_0,P_1)$ over $X$.

Associate to the principal difference bundle in step 1.1 the standard complex line. By [F2], its unit circle bundle is that principal bundle. The diagonal central action defines the twist $P_0\otimes L=(P_0\times_X L)/U(1)$; evaluation of each difference map gives a Spin$^c$-equivariant isomorphism $P_0\otimes L(P_0,P_1)\cong P_1$. If $P_0\otimes L\cong P_0$, its difference bundle is trivial, so the action is free; the construction for arbitrary $P_1$ proves transitivity. Tensor product of line bundles gives the group law and pullback commutes with the fiberwise construction.

By [F3], the isomorphism class of the associated line $L$ is uniquely identified with $c_1(L)\in H^2(X;\mathbb Z)$, compatibly with tensor product and pullback. Thus the free transitive line-bundle action is precisely a free transitive $H^2(X;\mathbb Z)$ action and is natural under $f^*$. If $X$ is a point, $H^2(X;\mathbb Z)=0$ and the given lift is the only class in its torsor; no existence of an initial lift is asserted. AC is used only through [A1] and [F3].

preserving $f$ with compatible subdivisions allowed. In the resulting finite
union construction all intersections may be made full subcomplexes. The same
relative conclusion applies to a fixed corner-adapted triangulated closed neighbourhood piece
whose smaller protected subcomplex lies in its relative interior: fitting is
performed away from that protected subcomplex. No extension of arbitrary

Assume AC. Let $M$ be a compact $R$-oriented $n$-manifold with boundary $A$, for a commutative unital ring $R$. Cap with its relative fundamental class gives isomorphisms, for every integer $p$,
$$S_p:H^p(M;R)\xrightarrow{\sim}H_{n-p}(M,A;R),\qquad T_p:H^p(M,A;R)\xrightarrow{\sim}H_{n-p}(M;R).$$
Here both maps send a class $a$ to $a\cap[M,A]$ in the displayed target. Empty boundary recovers Poincaré duality. Disconnected and empty manifolds are included. AC is inherited only from the exhaustion and local universal-coefficient arguments in Poincaré duality.

For every subspace $A\subseteq X$ and abelian group $G$ there is an exact sequence
$$\cdots\to H^n(X,A;G)\xrightarrow{j}H^n(X;G)\xrightarrow{r}H^n(A;G)\xrightarrow{\partial}H^{n+1}(X,A;G)\to\cdots.$$
Here $j$ comes from including the relative cochains, $r$ is restriction, and the connector sends a cocycle class $[a]$ to $[\delta\widetilde a]$, for any cochain extension $\widetilde a$ of $a$ to $X$. Negative groups are zero, so the sequence begins $0\to H^0(X,A;G)\to H^0(X;G)\to H^0(A;G)$.

For $A\subseteq X$ there is an exact sequence
$$\cdots\to H_n(A;G)\to H_n(X;G)\to H_n(X,A;G)\xrightarrow{\delta}H_{n-1}(A;G)\to H_{n-1}(X;G)\to\cdots.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $R$ be a PID, $C$ a chain complex of free
$R$-modules, and $G$ an $R$-module. Then naturally
$$0\to\operatorname{Ext}^1_R(H_{n-1}C,G)\to H^n\operatorname{Hom}_R(C,G)\xrightarrow{\operatorname{ev}_n}\operatorname{Hom}_R(H_nC,G)\to0$$
is exact.

Assume the Axiom of Choice from [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. Let

$$
0\longrightarrow A\xrightarrow{i}B\xrightarrow{q}C\longrightarrow0
$$

be a short exact sequence of abelian groups. Applying singular cochains degree
by degree gives a short exact sequence of cochain complexes: injectivity on the
left follows from injectivity of $i$, and surjectivity on the right follows as
follows. A cochain is a function on the set $S_n(X)$ of singular $n$-simplices
by [[def-singular-cochain-complex-with-coefficients]]. For a $C$-valued
cochain $c$, AC is used exactly once to choose, simultaneously for every
$s\in S_n(X)$, an element of the nonempty fibre $q^{-1}(c(s))$. The resulting
function is a $B$-valued cochain $b$ with $q_*b=c$.

For a cocycle $c\in C^n(X;C)$ choose such a lift $b$. Since
$q_*(\delta b)=\delta c=0$, exactness gives a unique
$a\in C^{n+1}(X;A)$ satisfying $i_*a=\delta b$. The **Bockstein connecting
operation** is

$$
\beta\colon H^n(X;C)\longrightarrow H^{n+1}(X;A),\qquad \beta[c]=[a].
$$

This is the coefficient-sequence analogue of the cochain connector in
[[thm-long-exact-sequence-of-a-pair-in-singular-cohomology]]. Its independence
of $b$ and $c$ is proved in the next lemma.

For an integer $m\geq1$, two Bocksteins must be distinguished:

- the **integral Bockstein**
  $\widetilde\beta\colon H^n(X;\mathbb Z/m)\to H^{n+1}(X;\mathbb Z)$ comes
  from $0\to\mathbb Z\xrightarrow{m}\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z/m\to0$;
- the **mod-$m$ Bockstein**
  $\beta\colon H^n(X;\mathbb Z/m)\to H^{n+1}(X;\mathbb Z/m)$ comes from

the required cochain lift without AC. If $X$ is empty, or if $n<0$, the source
cochain group is zero and the lift is unique. When $m=1$ both cyclic
Bocksteins have zero source and hence are the zero operation. The mod-$m$
target is also zero, whereas the integral target $H^{n+1}(X;\mathbb Z)$ need
not vanish.

Assume AC and the hypotheses and notation of
[[def-bockstein-connecting-operation]]. The class $\beta[c]$ is independent
of the chosen $B$-cochain lift of $c$ and of the cocycle representing $[c]$.

For continuous $f:X\to Y$ and a commutative unital ring $R$, pullback on singular cohomology satisfies
$$f^*(a\smile b)=f^*a\smile f^*b,\qquad f^*(1)=1.$$
Cup product is associative already on cochains. Consequently $f^*:H^*(Y;R)\to H^*(X;R)$ is a unital graded-ring homomorphism. Homotopic maps give the same homomorphism.

Assume AC. Let $M$ be an $R$-oriented boundaryless $n$-manifold, with $R$ commutative unital; manifolds are Hausdorff and second countable here. Then cap with the compatible compact orientation classes gives isomorphisms
$$D_M:H_c^p(M;R)\xrightarrow{\sim}H_{n-p}(M;R)$$
for every integer $p$, including disconnected, noncompact and empty $M$.

Naturality means that for an open inclusion $i:U\hookrightarrow M$ with restricted orientation, $D_M e=i_*D_U$, where $e$ is extension of compact supports. For compact $M$, $H_c^p(M;R)=H^p(M;R)$ canonically and $D_M(a)=a\cap[M]$. For arbitrary $M$ the isomorphism is the direct sum of those on its components. AC is used in the countable coordinate-neighborhood selection for exhaustion and in the local universal-coefficient proof.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $J=J_1\cup\cdots\cup J_n$ be an oriented link of $n\ge1$ smooth components in $S^3$. Choose pairwise disjoint closed tubular neighborhoods $N(J_i)$, let $X=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}(\bigcup_iN(J_i))$, and let $\mu_i$ be the positive meridian of $J_i$. Let $\lambda_i$ be the longitude parallel to $J_i$ with zero self-linking. Alexander duality identifies $H_1(X;\mathbb Z)$ with $\mathbb Z^n$ on the meridian basis $[\mu_1],\ldots,[\mu_n]$; for $i\ne j$, define $\operatorname{lk}_{S^3}(J_i,J_j)$ to be the $j$-th coordinate of $[\lambda_i]$, the usual oriented linking number. Use the boundary-torus intersection convention $\mu_i\mathbin{\cdot}\lambda_i=+1$. Give $J_i$ an integer framing $f_i$ and fill along $\delta_i=\lambda_i+f_i\mu_i$. Let $A$ be the symmetric integer matrix with $A_{ii}=f_i$ and $A_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}_{S^3}(J_i,J_j)$ for $i\ne j$. Assume $\det A\ne0$, and let $Y$ be the resulting oriented surgery manifold, oriented as the boundary of the 4-dimensional surgery handlebody with outward normal first. Then $H_1(Y;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z^n/A\mathbb Z^n$. For torsion classes $[C],[D]\in H_1(Y;\mathbb Z)$ represented by oriented 1-cycles, choose $m>0$ and an integral 2-chain $F$ with $\partial F=mC$ and define $\lambda_Y([C],[D])=(F\mathbin{\cdot}D)/m\pmod{\mathbb Z}$, where the intersection is signed by the orientation of $Y$. $$
\lambda_Y([x],[y])=-x^TA^{-1}y\pmod{\mathbb Z}.

Assume AC. Let $E\to X$ be an oriented real vector bundle over a path-connected paracompact Hausdorff compactly generated weak Hausdorff space of CW homotopy type, and suppose one numerable Spin$^c$ lift of its oriented frame bundle is given. Among numerable Spin$^c$ lifts of that same frame bundle, isomorphism classes form a torsor for $H^2(X;\mathbb Z)$: tensoring a lift by a complex line bundle defines a free and transitive action, identified with $H^2(X;\mathbb Z)$ by the first Chern class. For a continuous map $f:X\to Z$ between bases with these hypotheses and an oriented bundle $E_Z\to Z$, the pullback action on lifts of $f^*E_Z\to X$ is equivariant for $f^*:H^2(Z;\mathbb Z)\to H^2(X;\mathbb Z)$.

Assume AC. Let $M$ be a compact connected oriented smooth four-manifold with nonempty connected boundary $Y$, a specified Riemannian metric, and a Spin$^c(4)$ lift $P$ of its oriented tangent frame bundle. Give $Y$ the outward-normal-first orientation. The outward unit normal identifies $TM|_Y$ with $\mathbb R\oplus TY$. Restricting $P$ to $Y$ and reducing to frames with first vector that normal constructs a Spin$^c(3)$ lift $\operatorname{res}P$ of $TY$.

This construction induces a bijection between Spin$^c$ lift classes of $\mathbb R\oplus TY$ and those of $TY$, inverse to extension by $\operatorname{Spin}^c(3)\hookrightarrow\operatorname{Spin}^c(4)$. For every complex line bundle $L\to M$ there is a natural isomorphism
$$\operatorname{res}(P\otimes L)\cong(\operatorname{res}P)\otimes L|_Y.$$
Consequently, with the actual $H^2$ torsor actions, boundary restriction is equivariant for $H^2(M;\mathbb Z)\to H^2(Y;\mathbb Z)$. The determinant line of $\operatorname{res}P$ is the restriction of that of $P$; its change under a line twist is twice the line's first Chern class, while the torsor action is by the line's first Chern class itself. No Spin$^c$ existence or Floer map is asserted.

Assume AC. Let $B$ be a compact connected oriented smooth four-manifold with $H_*(B;\mathbb Q)\cong H_*(\mathrm{point};\mathbb Q)$. Then the oriented tangent frame bundle of $B$ admits a Spin$^c$ lift.

derivations.claim: Since $B$ has finite CW type by [F1] and has zero positive rational homology, each $H_i(B;\mathbb Z)$ for $i>0$ is finite. Put $a=|H_1(B;\mathbb Z)|$ and $b=|H_2(B;\mathbb Z)|$. The UCT [F3] gives $|H^2(B;\mathbb Z)|=a$ and $|H^3(B;\mathbb Z)|=b$, because the Hom terms from finite groups vanish and $\operatorname{Ext}^1(\mathbb Z/m,\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z/m$. Poincare-Lefschetz duality [F2] gives $|H^2(B,Y;\mathbb Z)|=b$ and $|H^3(B,Y;\mathbb Z)|=a$.

In the pair sequence, $H^1(Y;\mathbb Z)=0$ because $Y$ is a rational homology sphere and its first integral cohomology is $\operatorname{Hom}(H_1(Y),\mathbb Z)$. Thus $H^2(B,Y)\to H^2(B)$ is injective. Also $H^3(Y;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$, so the map from the finite group $H^3(B;\mathbb Z)$ to $H^3(Y;\mathbb Z)$ is zero; exactness makes $H^3(B,Y)\to H^3(B)$ surjective. It follows that the restriction image $M$ has order $a/b$, and that $H^2(Y)/M$ has order $a/b$. Hence $|H^2(Y)|=(a/b)^2$ and $|M|^2=|H^2(Y)|=|H_1(Y)|$, the last equality following from UCT and Poincare duality for the rational homology sphere.

For any $m\in M$, choose $u\in H^2(B;\mathbb Z)$ restricting to $m$, and let $c$ be an integral cocycle representing $u$. Since $H^2(B;\mathbb Q)=0$, the rational cocycle $c$ is $\delta q$ for a rational $1$-cochain $q$; reducing $q$ modulo $\mathbb Z$ gives a cocycle $v\in H^1(B;\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z)$ with $\beta(v)=u$. It is unique because $H^1(B;\mathbb Q)=0$. Restriction of this cochain lift gives $\beta(v|_Y)=m$. For $Y$, both $H^1(Y;\mathbb Q)$ and $H^2(Y;\mathbb Q)$ vanish, so the same coefficient sequence proves that $\beta:H^1(Y;\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z)\to H^2(Y;\mathbb Z)$ is an isomorphism. By UCT, $H^1(Y;\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z)\cong\operatorname{Hom}(H_1(Y),\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z)$; by Poincare duality, $H^2(Y;\mathbb Z)\cong H_1(Y;\mathbb Z)$. Cup evaluation is therefore the perfect character-evaluation pairing under these identifications. If $X,D$ are torsion $1$-cycles with $mX=\partial F$, the cochain represented by the rational bounding chain $F/m$, reduced modulo integral cochains, is $\beta^{-1}(\mathrm{PD}^{-1}[X])$; its evaluation against $\mathrm{PD}^{-1}[D]$ is $F\cdot D/m$ modulo $\mathbb Z$. Thus this cohomological formula agrees with the chain linking form up to the global orientation sign, which does not change annihilators.

If $x\in M$ is the restriction of $w\in H^2(B;\mathbb Z)$, naturality of cup product [F5] gives $\lambda_Y(m,x)=\langle v|_Y\smile w|_Y,[Y]\rangle=\langle v\smile w,i_*[Y]\rangle=0$, since $i_*[Y]=0$ in $H_3(B;\mathbb Z)$ by the homology pair sequence: $[Y]$ is the boundary of the relative fundamental class $[B,Y]$. Therefore $M\subseteq M^\perp$. For a nonsingular finite pairing on a group $G$, restriction of characters $G\to\operatorname{Hom}(G,\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z)$ to $\operatorname{Hom}(M,\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z)$ is onto. To see this, extend a character from a subgroup $H$ one generator $g$ at a time: if the least $n>0$ with $ng\in H$ is fixed, choose $z\in\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z$ with $nz=f(ng)$ (possible because multiplication by $n$ is onto), and set $f'(h+kg)=f(h)+kz$; the relation $ng\in H$ makes $f'$ well defined. Since $G$ is finite this process terminates. Hence $|M^\perp|=|G|/|M|$. Apply this with $G=H^2(Y;\mathbb Z)$ and use step 2.1 to obtain $|M^\perp|=|M|$. Thus $M=M^\perp$.

By [F7], choose a Spin$^c$ structure on $B$. Then [F6] makes the Spin$^c$ structures on $B$ an affine $H^2(B;\mathbb Z)$-space. Restriction is equivariant, so the image of this nonempty affine space is one affine coset of the image subgroup $M$. This proves the extension-set assertion. If $M=0$, the same sequence gives $|H^2(Y)|=1$, so the trivial subgroup is its own annihilator; the empty-boundary case is excluded by the connected-boundary hypothesis.

Heegaard-move isomorphisms preserve this grading and commute with the minus/infinity/plus sequence. A smooth connected Spin$^c$ cobordism between such manifolds induces infinity and plus maps, compatible with that sequence, homogeneous of degree $(c_1(\mathfrak s)^2-2\chi(W)-3\sigma(W))/4$. These maps are obtained from the fixed-Spin$^c$ triangle counts and the one- and three-handle maps, independently of their handle presentation. Here the Chern square uses the rational relative lift of the boundary-torsion Chern class.

For every closed connected oriented rational homology three-sphere $Y$ and Spin$^c$ structure $\mathfrak t$, the absolutely graded infinity group $HF^\infty(Y,\mathfrak t;\mathbb F_2)$ is a single free Laurent tower. If $W:Y_0\to Y_1$ is a smooth connected rational homology cobordism between rational homology spheres, then for each fixed Spin$^c$ structure $\mathfrak s$ on $W$ the infinity map is a degree-zero isomorphism. The corresponding plus map commutes with the infinity-to-plus maps. This conclusion concerns each individual extending Spin$^c$ structure, including nonprimitive handle attachments and torsion labels.

derivations.claim: The minus chain complex is finite free over $\mathbb F_2[U]$, with generators $[\mathbf x,-1]$ for the finitely many intersection points in $\mathfrak t$. Its homology is finitely generated and its localization is the infinity homology, since localization is exact and the localized differentials are identical. Thus the graded image $L$ of $HF^-\to R\rho$ is nonzero. Its degrees are bounded above by the largest degree of a minus-chain generator. The set of integers $j$ with $U^j\rho\in L$ is consequently nonempty, bounded below, and closed under addition of nonnegative integers. If $a$ is its minimum, that set is exactly $\{a,a+1,\ldots\}$. Every homogeneous element of the Laurent tower is a monomial multiple of $\rho$, and the image is graded; hence $L=U^a\mathbb F_2[U]\rho$.

The long exact sequence of the actual short exact sequence $CF^-\to CF^\infty\to CF^+$ identifies the image in plus homology, with its grading, as $R\rho/U^a\mathbb F_2[U]\rho$. Its nonzero homogeneous elements have exponents $j<a$, so their least degree is $\deg\rho-2(a-1)$, attained at $U^{a-1}\rho$. Sending the standard tower element $U^k$ to $U^{k+a-1}\rho$ identifies the image with $R/U\mathbb F_2[U]$ shifted by this least degree. Multiplying any individual element sufficiently many times by $U$ kills it, while decreasing exponents supplies a preimage under any power of $U$. This proves all the tower assertions.

The pointed-move maps preserve absolute grading and the minus/infinity/plus exact sequence, so they carry $L$ onto the corresponding image lattice and induce grading-preserving tower isomorphisms. Therefore the least degree is independent of the diagram and auxiliary data. Choosing $U^b\rho$ instead changes $a$ to $a-b$ and $\deg\rho$ to $\deg\rho-2b$, leaving that degree unchanged. In the genus-zero diagram of $S^3$ there is one generator $[\mathbf x_0,0]$ of degree zero, no nonconstant disks, and minus lattice $U\mathbb F_2[U][\mathbf x_0,0]$. Here $a=1$, giving $d(S^3)=0$.

Let $B$ be a compact connected oriented smooth four-manifold with $H_*(B;\mathbb Q)\cong H_*(\mathrm{point};\mathbb Q)$ and connected rational homology sphere boundary $Y$. Choose a smoothly embedded closed four-ball $D$ in its interior and put $W=B\setminus\operatorname{int}D$. With the induced orientation,
$$\partial W=-S^3\sqcup Y.$$
The manifold $W$ is connected, $H_j(W;\mathbb Q)$ is $\mathbb Q$ for $j=0,3$ and zero otherwise, and both inclusions $S^3\to W$, $Y\to W$ induce isomorphisms on rational homology in every degree. Its rational homological Euler characteristic is zero and its rational intersection module $H_2(W;\mathbb Q)$ is zero. Consequently its signature is zero, and the square of every covector with respect to that zero intersection module is zero. These assertions hold also for the reversed cobordism $-W$ from $Y$ to $S^3$, and use no choice principle.

The last square assertion refers to the intersection-form covector convention; the lemma supplies no Floer cobordism map, absolute grading formula, or Spin-c existence theorem.

For a closed connected oriented rational homology three-sphere and each Spin$^c$ structure, the pointed minus, infinity and plus Heegaard Floer complexes over $\mathbb F_2$ admit an absolute rational grading, independent of the surgery presentation, extending their relative Maslov grading, with $\deg U=-2$ and $\deg[\mathbf x_0,0]=0$ for the standard generator of $S^3$. Heegaard-move isomorphisms preserve this grading and commute with the minus/infinity/plus sequence. A smooth connected Spin$^c$ cobordism between such manifolds induces infinity and plus maps, compatible with that sequence, homogeneous of degree $(c_1(\mathfrak s)^2-2\chi(W)-3\sigma(W))/4$. These maps are obtained from the fixed-Spin$^c$ triangle counts and the one- and three-handle maps, independently of their handle presentation. Here the Chern square uses the rational relative lift of the boundary-torsion Chern class.

For every closed connected oriented rational homology three-sphere $Y$ and Spin$^c$ structure $\mathfrak t$, the absolutely graded infinity group $HF^\infty(Y,\mathfrak t;\mathbb F_2)$ is a single free Laurent tower. If $W:Y_0\to Y_1$ is a smooth connected rational homology cobordism between rational homology spheres, then for each fixed Spin$^c$ structure $\mathfrak s$ on $W$ the infinity map is a degree-zero isomorphism. The corresponding plus map commutes with the infinity-to-plus maps. This conclusion concerns each individual extending Spin$^c$ structure, including nonprimitive handle attachments and torsion labels.

For every closed connected oriented rational homology three-sphere $Y$ and Spin$^c$ structure $\mathfrak t$, the standard Heegaard Floer groups $HF^\infty(Y,\mathfrak t)$ and $HF^+(Y,\mathfrak t)$ constructed from admissible pointed Heegaard diagrams are independent, up to grading-preserving isomorphism, of the diagram and regular auxiliary data. The image of $HF^\infty\to HF^+$ is a graded plus tower, isomorphic as an $\mathbb F_2[U]$-module to $\mathbb F_2[U,U^{-1}]/U\mathbb F_2[U]$ with an absolute rational grading shift and with $U$ of degree $-2$. Its nonzero homogeneous elements have a least grading; this least grading $d(Y,\mathfrak t)$ exists and is independent of choices. Every tower element is $U$-torsion and is divisible by every power of $U$. The normalization is $d(S^3,\mathfrak t_0)=0$.

Put $R=\mathbb F_2[U]$, with $\deg U=-2$. For $i=1,2$ let $\Lambda_i=\mathbb F_2[U,U^{-1}]$ with $\deg_i U^n=a_i-2n$, $a_i\in\mathbb Q$, and let $\pi_i:\Lambda_i\to M_i$ be degree-zero $R$-linear maps to graded $R$-modules with nonzero proper kernels. Let $d_i$ be the least degree of a nonzero homogeneous element of $\operatorname{im}\pi_i$.

Suppose $F:\Lambda_1\to\Lambda_2$ is an $R$-linear isomorphism homogeneous of degree $\Delta\in\mathbb Q$, and $G:M_1\to M_2$ is an $R$-linear map of that same degree such that $G\pi_1=\pi_2F$. Then
$$d_2\ge d_1+\Delta.$$
If there are also maps in the reverse direction of degree $-\Delta$ satisfying the same hypotheses and commuting with $\pi_1,\pi_2$, then $d_2=d_1+\Delta$; those reverse maps need not be inverses of $F,G$. In particular, commuting comparisons in both directions with degree zero force equal bottom degrees. These are choice-free algebraic statements; no Floer map, Laurent-tower hypothesis or geometric degree formula is supplied by this lemma.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

For an integer $n\ge1$, **complex projective space** is the set of complex lines in $\mathbb C^{n+1}$ with the quotient topology
$$\mathbb P^n(\mathbb C):=(\mathbb C^{n+1}\setminus\{0\})/\mathbb C^\times,\qquad [z_0:\cdots:z_n]:=\mathbb C^\times(z_0,\ldots,z_n).$$
The quotient projection is continuous and surjective. Its restriction to the unit sphere $S^{2n+1}\subset\mathbb C^{n+1}$ is still surjective, so $\mathbb P^n(\mathbb C)$ is compact. It is Hausdorff: the map sending a nonzero vector $z$ to the orthogonal projection $zz^*/\lVert z\rVert^2$ is continuous and constant on each complex line, hence descends by the quotient topology to a continuous injection from $\mathbb P^n(\mathbb C)$ into the Hausdorff space of complex matrices. A continuous injection from a compact space to a Hausdorff space is a homeomorphism onto its image.

For open $V\subseteq\mathbb C^r$, a map $H:V\to\mathbb C^s$ is **holomorphic** if at every $a\in V$ there is a complex-linear map $A_a:\mathbb C^r\to\mathbb C^s$ such that $H(a+h)=H(a)+A_a h+R_a(h)$ with $\lVert R_a(h)\rVert/\lVert h\rVert\to0$ as $h\to0$, $h\ne0$. When $r=1$, this is equivalent to each component being holomorphic in the sense of [[def-complex-differentiability-holomorphic-and-entire]], since a finite vector of scalar difference quotients converges exactly when each component does. A complex atlas consists of charts into $\mathbb C^n$ with holomorphic transitions in both directions.

For $j\in\{0,\ldots,n\}$ let $U_j:=\{[z_0:\cdots:z_n]:z_j\ne0\}$. These open sets cover projective space: their inverse images under the quotient projection are the open saturated sets where $z_j\ne0$. The **standard chart** is
$$\varphi_j:U_j\longrightarrow\mathbb C^n,\qquad [z_0:\cdots:z_n]\longmapsto (z_0/z_j,\ldots,\widehat{z_j/z_j},\ldots,z_n/z_j),$$
where the $j$th coordinate is omitted. It is well defined under rescaling. The coordinate-ratio map on the inverse image of $U_j$ is continuous and constant on each quotient fibre, so the quotient topology makes $\varphi_j$ continuous; its inverse inserts $1$ in the $j$th position and is continuous by composition with the quotient projection. Hence it is a homeomorphism. On $U_j\cap U_k$ the transition from the $j$th chart to the $k$th chart sends each coordinate $w_\ell=z_\ell/z_j$ ($\ell\ne j$) to $w_\ell/w_k$ for $\ell\ne k$, with the omitted $j$th coordinate equal to $1/w_k$. To check holomorphy at $a$ with $a_k\ne0$, set $a_j=1$ and $h_j=0$ for the omitted source coordinate. Each target coordinate has the expansion $(a_\ell+h_\ell)/(a_k+h_k)=a_\ell/a_k+h_\ell/a_k-a_\ell h_k/a_k^2+O(\lVert h\rVert^2)$ for $\ell\ne k$. The linear term is complex-linear, and the remainder estimate follows by expanding the reciprocal at the nonzero $a_k$. The inverse transition has the same form, so both are holomorphic. Thus these charts make $\mathbb P^n(\mathbb C)$ a complex manifold of complex dimension $n$ and a topological manifold of real dimension $2n$ in the sense of [[def-topological-manifold-without-boundary]]. The finite chart cover by second-countable copies of $\mathbb C^n$ gives a countable base. Its rational transition functions have smooth real coordinate expressions on their domains, so the atlas also defines the smooth structure in the sense of [[def-smooth-manifold]]. The space is path-connected: distinct lines represented by $u,v$ give the path $t\mapsto[(1-t)u+tv]$, whose vector never vanishes because $u,v$ are linearly independent; equal lines give a constant path. In particular, $\mathbb P^1(\mathbb C)$ is a Riemann surface in the sense of [[def-riemann-surface-and-holomorphic-atlas]].

A map $F:X\to\mathbb P^n(\mathbb C)$ from a Riemann surface is **holomorphic** when it is continuous and every component of each chart expression $\varphi_j\circ F$, written in a local coordinate of $X$, is holomorphic on the open set $F^{-1}(U_j)$. On an overlap, the new components are $f_\ell/f_k$ and $1/f_k$, where the $f_\ell$ are the old components and $f_k\ne0$. The scalar quotient rule gives their holomorphy ([[thm-algebra-of-complex-derivatives]]), so it suffices to check one target chart locally. Changing the source coordinate composes each scalar component with a one-variable holomorphic chart transition, where [[thm-chain-rule-for-complex-derivatives]] applies ([[def-holomorphic-and-meromorphic-map-of-riemann-surfaces]]). A **projective line** is the image in $\mathbb P^n(\mathbb C)$ of a two-dimensional complex subspace of $\mathbb C^{n+1}$. Every invertible linear map of $\mathbb C^{n+1}$ induces a holomorphic projective linear transformation: in source and target standard charts its coordinates are ratios of affine-linear functions with nonzero denominator, and the same reciprocal expansion gives a complex-linear derivative; these transformations act transitively on $\mathbb P^n(\mathbb C)$.

$$a\longmapsto\pi^*a\smile u_\xi:H^k(B;R)\xrightarrow{\cong}H^{k+n}(D(\xi),S(\xi);R)$$

The finite supplied-trivializing-cover theorem is a choice-free special case.

section $o=(o_b)$.  For the inclusion of pairs
$$i_b:(D(\xi_b),S(\xi_b))\longrightarrow(D(\xi),S(\xi)),$$

$$u_\xi\in H^n(D(\xi),S(\xi);R)$$

Relative singular cochains make every restriction $i_b^*$ well typed.  This
is a normalization condition only: the definition asserts neither existence
nor uniqueness, which are proved later.  For $B=\varnothing$ the condition is
vacuous and the unique class in the zero relative group is normalized.  In

u_Z=TM|_Z/TZ$ in tangent-first order: $\det TM|_Z=\det TZ\otimes\det
u_Z$. Choose a smooth metric and a tubular chart whose differential induces the identity on this normal quotient; restrict to a sufficiently small closed disk bundle. Such normalized charts exist by the construction in [[thm-tubular-neighbourhood-theorem-in-a-smooth-ambient-manifold]].

The normalized Thom class $u_
u\in H^r(D(
u),S(
u);R)$ corresponds to a class $\alpha\in H^r(M,M\setminus Z;R)$ by the punctured-fibre comparison and tubular excision. Write $ ar\alpha\in H^r(M;R)$ for its relative-to-absolute image. Then
$$ ar\alpha\cap[M]=(-1)^{rz}(i_Z)_*[Z]\in H_z(M;R).$$
Equivalently, $ ar\alpha=(-1)^{rz}D_M^{-1}((i_Z)_*[Z])$. The sign is the shuffle from tangent-first coordinates to normal-first cap evaluation. Over $\mathbb F_2$ all orientations are canonical and the sign disappears. A relative class capped directly with the absolute $[M]$ instead has relative homology as target; the displayed formula uses $ ar\alpha$.

Let $M$ be a compact boundaryless $n$-manifold with a specified $R$-orientation $\mu$, where $R$ is a commutative unital ring. Its **fundamental class** is
$$[M]=[M]_M\in H_n(M,M\setminus M;R)=H_n(M;R),$$
using [[lem-compatible-local-orientation-classes-exist-over-compact-subsets]] with the compact support $K=M$. The final equality holds at the chain-complex level: $C_*(\varnothing;R)=0$, so quotienting by it leaves $C_*(M;R)$. The cited lemma proves existence and uniqueness of this class with point restriction $\mu_x$ at every $x\in M$. Thus the notation denotes a class determined by the supplied orientation, not an arbitrary generator chosen afterward.

The same lemma gives finitely many open-and-closed components $M_1,\ldots,M_k$ and the restriction isomorphism
$$H_n(M;R)\longrightarrow\bigoplus_{j=1}^k H_n(M,M\setminus M_j;R).$$
The summand on the right identifies with $H_n(M_j;R)$: apply [[thm-excision-for-singular-homology]] to remove the closed set $M\setminus M_j$, which is the entire open relative subspace. The resulting pair is $(M_j,\varnothing)$. Under this identification $[M]$ corresponds to the finite tuple of the component fundamental classes.

If the orientation is negated on one component, its new fundamental-class summand is the negative of its old one. Indeed restriction is linear, so the negative class restricts to $-\mu_x$ at all points of that component, and uniqueness in the compact-set lemma identifies it with the new class. The other component summands are unchanged. In characteristic two this negation can leave the orientation and class unchanged; no distinction between $\mu$ and $-\mu$ is imposed when they are equal.

For empty $M$ the fundamental class is $0$ in the zero homology group, with an empty direct sum. For $R=0$ the unique orientation gives the zero class. A compact zero-manifold has finitely many singleton components, and its fundamental zero-cycle has at each point the coefficient prescribed by its local module generator. The definition requires a supplied orientation and uses no AC or simultaneous choice of one orientation per component.

Assume AC. Let $M$ be an $R$-oriented boundaryless $n$-manifold, with $R$ commutative unital; manifolds are Hausdorff and second countable here. Then cap with the compatible compact orientation classes gives isomorphisms
$$D_M:H_c^p(M;R)\xrightarrow{\sim}H_{n-p}(M;R)$$
for every integer $p$, including disconnected, noncompact and empty $M$.

Naturality means that for an open inclusion $i:U\hookrightarrow M$ with restricted orientation, $D_M e=i_*D_U$, where $e$ is extension of compact supports. For compact $M$, $H_c^p(M;R)=H^p(M;R)$ canonically and $D_M(a)=a\cap[M]$. For arbitrary $M$ the isomorphism is the direct sum of those on its components. AC is used in the countable coordinate-neighborhood selection for exhaustion and in the local universal-coefficient proof.

Assume AC. Let $M$ be a closed oriented smooth $n$-manifold and let $A^a,B^b\subseteq M$ be closed oriented embedded submanifolds with $a+b=n$. Write $[A]=(i_A)_*[A]_A$, $[B]=(i_B)_*[B]_B$, and $\mathrm{PD}[A]=D_M^{-1}([A])$, $\mathrm{PD}[B]=D_M^{-1}([B])$. In the cohomology-first, front-evaluation cap and cup conventions,
$$I(A,B)=\langle\mathrm{PD}[A]\smile\mathrm{PD}[B],[M]\rangle.$$
For nontransverse submanifolds $I(A,B)$ is computed by a transverse map homotopic to $i_A$; no embedded representative for that map is required. Over $\mathbb F_2$ the same formula holds without orientability. Consequently this geometric number depends only on the represented homology classes, with the factor order of [[def-local-oriented-intersection-sign]].

If $f,g:X\to Y$ are homotopic continuous maps, then for every $n\geq 0$ and
every abelian group $G$ the induced homomorphisms on singular homology agree:
$$H_n(f_\#)=H_n(g_\#):H_n^{\mathrm{sing}}(X;G)\to H_n^{\mathrm{sing}}(Y;G).$$

Let $M$ be an oriented smooth $n$-manifold and let $f:X^x\to M$ and $g:Z^z\to M$ be smooth maps from oriented smooth manifolds, with $x+z=n$ and $f,g$ transverse in the sense of [[def-transverse-smooth-maps]]. Let $a\in X$, $b\in Z$ satisfy $f(a)=g(b)=y$. Then $T_aX\oplus T_bZ$ and $T_yM$ have the same dimension, and transversality says that

$$(df_a,dg_b):T_aX\oplus T_bZ\longrightarrow T_yM,\qquad (v,w)\mapsto df_a(v)+dg_b(w),$$

is surjective, hence a linear isomorphism ([[def-transverse-linear-subspaces]]); the sum is direct because the dimensions add up. The ordered direct sum $T_aX\oplus T_bZ$ carries the product orientation with the first factor $T_aX$ and the second factor $T_bZ$ ([[def-product-orientation]]), and the three tangent spaces carry their manifold orientations ([[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]]).

The **local oriented intersection sign** $\varepsilon(a,b)\in\{+1,-1\}$ is $+1$ when this isomorphism carries the product orientation of $T_aX\oplus T_bZ$ to the orientation of $T_yM$, and $-1$ otherwise; equivalently it is the orientation sign of the induced isomorphism of determinant lines ([[def-determinant-line-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]], [[def-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]).

For transverse oriented embedded submanifolds $A^a,B^b\subseteq M$ with $a+b=n$ one takes $f$ and $g$ to be the inclusion maps ([[def-transverse-embedded-submanifolds]]); the sign at $p\in A\cap B$ then compares $T_pA\oplus T_pB\to T_pM$ with $A$ first. The empty intersection is allowed and carries no signs. In dimension zero the sign compares the two orientation rays directly, and for $x=z=n=0$ it is $\varepsilon_X(a)\varepsilon_Z(b)\varepsilon_M(y)$, the product of the two source point signs and the ambient point sign. The factor order is part of the definition: with the two factors exchanged the signs are multiplied by $(-1)^{ab}$, exactly the graded-commutativity sign measured later on this page by the factor-interchange theorem. No compactness, closedness hypothesis or choice axiom is used in this local definition.

Let $M$ be a closed oriented smooth $n$-manifold and let $A^a,B^b\subseteq M$ be closed oriented embedded submanifolds with $a+b=n$. Using the oriented intersection number of [[def-oriented-intersection-number]] (whose source is the compact submanifold and whose target is the closed submanifold, first factor first), set $$\langle A,B\rangle_M:=I(A,B)=I(i_A,B)\in\mathbb Z,$$ where $i_A:A\hookrightarrow M$ is the inclusion and $I(i_A,B)$ is evaluated on any smooth map homotopic to $i_A$ and transverse to $B$; when $A$ and $B$ are transverse this is the finite signed count $\sum_{p\in A\cap B}\varepsilon(p)$ of the local signs of [[def-local-oriented-intersection-sign]]. For non-transverse $A,B$ the value is the common value on all such transverse representatives, by [[thm-oriented-intersection-number-is-homotopy-invariant]]. With $\mathbb F_2$ coefficients the same construction with the mod 2 intersection number [[def-mod-two-intersection-number]] defines $\langle A,B\rangle_{2}\in\mathbb F_2$ without orientability of $A,B$ or $M$; there [[thm-mod-two-intersection-number-is-homotopy-invariant]] supplies the same independence. The number depends only on the homotopy classes of the two inclusions, so replacing a factor by a homotopic submanifold, or by a homotopic embedding of the same manifold, leaves it unchanged. The factor order is part of the definition: [[thm-intersection-number-under-factor-interchange]] gives $\langle B,A\rangle=(-1)^{ab}\langle A,B\rangle$ and $\langle B,A\rangle_2=\langle A,B\rangle_2$. No claim is made yet that the number depends only on the homology classes of $A$ and $B$ (homology invariance is proved in [[thm-geometric-intersection-equals-the-poincare-dual-cup-pairing]]; [[lem-geometric-intersection-descends-through-oriented-cobordism-of-cycles]] separately proves bordism invariance), nor that every homology class has an embedded representative (see [[rem-not-every-homology-class-is-represented-by-an-embedded-submanifold-integrally]]). Countable Choice is inherited from the transverse-representative selection in [[def-countable-choice]]; the finite signed counts themselves are choice-free.

Let $X$ be a compact oriented smooth $x$-manifold without boundary, let $M$ be an oriented smooth $n$-manifold without boundary, and let $Z\subseteq M$ be a closed oriented embedded $z$-submanifold with $x+z=n$ ([[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]]). For a smooth $f:X\to M$ transverse to $Z$, the **oriented intersection number** is the finite sum

$$I(f,Z):=\sum_{p\in f^{-1}(Z)}\varepsilon(p)\in\mathbb Z,$$

with the local signs of [[def-local-oriented-intersection-sign]]; the sum is finite by [[lem-compact-transverse-complementary-intersections-are-finite]]. For an arbitrary smooth $g:X\to M$, choose a transverse $f$ homotopic to $g$ ([[thm-transversality-homotopy-theorem]], under Countable Choice; the homotopy is a smooth family in the sense of [[def-smooth-family-of-maps-and-evaluation-map]]) and set $I(g,Z):=I(f,Z)$; independence of the choice is [[thm-oriented-intersection-number-is-homotopy-invariant]], not assumed here. For compact oriented complementary-dimensional submanifolds $A,B\subseteq M$, where one is compact and the other closed, one sets $I(A,B):=I(i_A,B)$ with $i_A$ the inclusion, so the first factor is the submanifold $A$. If the source is not compact, or the target submanifold is not closed, the sum may fail to be finite or invariant; the safe extension by properness with compact trace is recorded in the remark on properness later on this page. Countable Choice is assumed for selecting transverse representatives and for the classification used to prove independence of that selection; the signs, the finite sum and the empty case (which contributes $0$) are choice-free.

For transverse maps $f:X^x\to M$, $g:Z^z\to M$ with compact oriented boundaryless sources and $x+z=\dim M$, define $I(f,g)$ as the sum of the local signs of [[def-local-oriented-intersection-sign]] over $X\times_MZ$. This set is closed in the compact product because $M$ is Hausdorff, and discrete by [[def-transverse-complementary-dimensional-intersection-set]], so the sum is finite. If $g$ is an inclusion this recovers $I(f,Z)$. Ambient compactness is unnecessary in either construction.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $M$ be an oriented boundaryless smooth $n$-manifold and let $A^a\subseteq M$ be a compact boundaryless oriented embedded submanifold with $2a=n$. Orient $\nu_A=TM|_A/TA$ by the tangent-first rule. Choose a smooth bundle metric and a tubular chart $\varphi$ whose normal differential along the zero section is the identity, as constructed in [[thm-tubular-neighbourhood-theorem-in-a-smooth-ambient-manifold]]. Compactness of $A$ permits a uniform small disk bundle inside the tube. For any small smooth section $s$ transverse to the zero section, let $A_s=\varphi(s(A))$, oriented by the parametrization $\varphi\circ s:A\to A_s$. The **self-intersection number** is
$$A\cdot A:=I(A,A_s),$$
with $A$ first and $A_s$ second.

Every section is an embedding into its total space: projection is a left inverse, its differential is injective, and projection restricted to its graph is its continuous inverse. Composing with the tube therefore gives an embedding. The homotopy $\varphi(ts)$ consists of embeddings and joins the inclusion to the push-off. Compactness makes $A_s$ closed and the transverse count finite. Small transverse sections exist: extend local frame vectors to compactly supported sections by [[lem-every-vector-in-a-fibre-extends-to-a-compactly-supported-smooth-section]], take finitely many which span every fibre by compactness, and apply [[thm-parametric-transversality]] to their parameter-linear sum. The full evaluation is transverse because the parameter directions span every fibre. A good parameter can be chosen arbitrarily small, including the rank-zero case where every section is already transverse.

The same definition using [[def-mod-two-intersection-number]] gives $A\cdot_2A$ for any boundaryless ambient $M$ and any compact boundaryless embedded $A$ with $2a=n$, using no orientations. The numerical value is independent of the tube and small section: each push-off map is homotopic to the inclusion, and the two-map diagonal construction underlying [[thm-intersection-number-under-factor-interchange]] and [[thm-mod-two-intersection-number-is-homotopy-invariant]] makes the ordered count invariant under that homotopy. This argument requires no assertion that the tube-germ comparison is an isotopy. Under AC the integral Euler evaluation is proved in [[thm-self-intersection-is-the-euler-number-of-the-normal-bundle]]. The local signs and finite counts themselves require no choice.

Assume AC. Let $M$ be an oriented boundaryless smooth $n$-manifold, $A^a\subseteq M$ a compact boundaryless oriented embedded submanifold with $2a=n$, and let $
u_A=TM|_A/TA$ carry the orientation induced by $M$ and $A$ ([[prop-a-transverse-oriented-normal-bundle-orients-an-embedded-submanifold]]). Then the self-intersection number of [[def-self-intersection-number-of-an-oriented-submanifold]] is well defined and $$A\cdot A=\langle e(
u_A),[A]angle\in\mathbb Z,$$ where $e(
u_A)\in H^{a}(A;\mathbb Z)$ is the Euler class of [[def-euler-class-by-zero-section-pullback-of-the-thom-class]] and $[A]\in H_a(A;\mathbb Z)$ is the fundamental class. In particular the self-intersection number is independent of the tubular embedding and of the transverse push-off, and it is an invariant of the pair $(A,
u_A)$. For a rank-$r$ oriented bundle $E	o M$ with $M$ closed oriented of dimension $n=r$ and a transverse section $s$, the signed zero count equals $\langle e(E),[M]angle$; this is the form in which the theorem is applied below.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. An oriented lens space is an oriented closed $3$-manifold obtained by gluing two solid tori by an orientation-reversing boundary homeomorphism. For coprime integers $p>0$ and $q$, let $L(p,q)$ denote the oriented union of the exterior of the unknot in the oriented $3$-sphere and a solid torus whose meridian is identified with the slope $p[\mu_U]+q[\lambda_U]$ on the unknot exterior. Thus this library uses the convention $L(p,q)=E_U(p/q)$; no symbol $L(0,q)$ is assigned.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $J=J_1\cup\cdots\cup J_n$ be an oriented link of $n\ge1$ smooth components in $S^3$. Choose pairwise disjoint closed tubular neighborhoods $N(J_i)$, let $X=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}(\bigcup_iN(J_i))$, and let $\mu_i$ be the positive meridian of $J_i$. Let $\lambda_i$ be the longitude parallel to $J_i$ with zero self-linking. Alexander duality identifies $H_1(X;\mathbb Z)$ with $\mathbb Z^n$ on the meridian basis $[\mu_1],\ldots,[\mu_n]$; for $i\ne j$, define $\operatorname{lk}_{S^3}(J_i,J_j)$ to be the $j$-th coordinate of $[\lambda_i]$, the usual oriented linking number. Use the boundary-torus intersection convention $\mu_i\mathbin{\cdot}\lambda_i=+1$. Give $J_i$ an integer framing $f_i$ and fill along $\delta_i=\lambda_i+f_i\mu_i$. Let $A$ be the symmetric integer matrix with $A_{ii}=f_i$ and $A_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}_{S^3}(J_i,J_j)$ for $i\ne j$. Assume $\det A\ne0$, and let $Y$ be the resulting oriented surgery manifold, oriented as the boundary of the 4-dimensional surgery handlebody with outward normal first. Then $H_1(Y;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z^n/A\mathbb Z^n$. For torsion classes $[C],[D]\in H_1(Y;\mathbb Z)$ represented by oriented 1-cycles, choose $m>0$ and an integral 2-chain $F$ with $\partial F=mC$ and define $\lambda_Y([C],[D])=(F\mathbin{\cdot}D)/m\pmod{\mathbb Z}$, where the intersection is signed by the orientation of $Y$. If $x,y\in\mathbb Z^n$ are meridian-coordinate representatives of $[C],[D]$, then
$$
\lambda_Y([x],[y])=-x^TA^{-1}y\pmod{\mathbb Z}.
$$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

For every subspace $A\subseteq X$ and abelian group $G$ there is an exact sequence
$$\cdots\to H^n(X,A;G)\xrightarrow{j}H^n(X;G)\xrightarrow{r}H^n(A;G)\xrightarrow{\partial}H^{n+1}(X,A;G)\to\cdots.$$
Here $j$ comes from including the relative cochains, $r$ is restriction, and the connector sends a cocycle class $[a]$ to $[\delta\widetilde a]$, for any cochain extension $\widetilde a$ of $a$ to $X$. Negative groups are zero, so the sequence begins $0\to H^0(X,A;G)\to H^0(X;G)\to H^0(A;G)$.

Choose the filtration $\mathbb{CP}^0\subset P\subset\mathbb{CP}^2$ with $P=\{y=0\}\cong\mathbb{CP}^1$ and $\mathbb{CP}^0=[1:0:0]$. Its successive complements are $\mathbb C$ and $\mathbb C^2$, so the cellular boundary maps vanish for degree reasons and $H_2(\mathbb{CP}^2;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z[P]$, $H_4(\mathbb{CP}^2;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z[\mathbb{CP}^2]$; UCT gives free cohomology, and put $h=\mathrm{PD}[P]$. The projective maps $T_t([x:y:z])=[x:y+tx:z]$ ($0\le t\le1$) give a homotopy from the inclusion of $P$ to that of $P'=\{y=x\}$. The two lines meet transversely at $[0:0:1]$ with positive sign, since a complex-linear isomorphism between their tangent complex lines and the ambient complex plane has positive real determinant. By [F3], $[P]^2=1$. On the charts $s
e0$ and $t
e0$, the conic map $[s:t]\mapsto[s^2:st:t^2]$ has target coordinates $(u,u^2)$ with $u=t/s$ and $(v^2,v)$ with $v=s/t$, respectively; these recover the source coordinate and have injective derivatives. Its image is exactly $xz-y^2=0$: if $x
e0$ the point is $[1:y/x:(y/x)^2]$, and if $x=0$ then $y=0$ and the point is $[0:0:1]$. The same chart descriptions show the zero set is a smooth complex-oriented sphere and the map is an embedding. The line $P$ meets it at the two simple roots $st=0$, both transversely and positively in the complex orientations. Thus [F3] gives $[Q]\cdot[P]=2$; because $[P]$ generates $H_2$, this implies $[Q]=2[P]$, hence $[Q]\cdot[Q]=4$.

The normal Euler number of $Q$ is therefore $4$ by [F4]. Its unit normal circle bundle is the boundary of its tubular disk bundle. Compute its genus-one gluing directly from the conic charts, without assuming an Euler-to-surgery identification. In the chart $x=1$ write the surface as $(y,z)=(u,u^2)$ and use normal coordinate $n=z-y^2$. In the chart $z=1$ use normal coordinate $n'=x-y^2$. Their change is $n'=(z-y^2)/z^2$; differentiating in the normal direction on the conic gives $n'=u^{-4}n$ in the normal line bundle. On the equator $u=e^{i\varphi}$ its unit normal circle transition is therefore $\theta_N=\theta_S-4\varphi$. Each closed hemisphere has its actual displayed complex normal frame, so its unit circle bundle is $D^2\times S^1$, a solid torus. On their common torus let $m$ be the equator loop at fixed $\theta_S$, and $l$ the fiber loop. The southern solid-torus meridian is $m$, and the northern meridian is $m+4l$, since holding $\theta_N$ fixed gives that exact slope. Identify the southern solid torus with the standard unknot exterior by $l=\mu_U$, $m=\lambda_U$: its fiber is the core circle, while its base disk is the exterior meridian disk. The second filling slope is therefore $4\mu_U+\lambda_U$, with the global boundary orientation determined by the product identifications. If those identifications reverse the desired global orientation, reverse the orientation of the total space; the statement permits exactly that choice. Thus [F5] identifies the total circle bundle with $L(4,1)$ up to orientation, by an actual meridian calculation. The complement has the opposite boundary orientation to its tubular neighborhood in the complex-oriented projective plane; choose the orientation of $B_2$ as allowed in the Statement so its boundary agrees with the declared lens-space convention.

By [F2], the relative cohomology groups of $(\mathbb{CP}^2,B_2)$ are $\mathbb Z$ in degrees $2$ and $4$ and zero otherwise, since $Q\cong S^2$. The relative-to-absolute map in degree two sends the Thom generator to $\mathrm{PD}[Q]$: the normal-Thom sign is $(-1)^{2\cdot2}=+1$ by [F2]. By step 1.1, $[Q]=2[P]$, so this map is multiplication by $2$ under $h=\mathrm{PD}[P]$. For degree four, let $a$ be the positive generator of $H^2(Q;\mathbb Z)$, with $\langle a,[Q]\rangle=1$. The Thom image of $a$ evaluates on $[\mathbb{CP}^2]$ as $\langle a,[Q]\rangle$: excision reduces the evaluation to the normal disk fibers, and the normalized Thom class evaluates $+1$ on each such fiber by [F2]. Thus the degree-four relative-to-absolute map sends a generator to a generator and is an isomorphism.

By [F6], the cohomology long exact sequence of the pair gives $H^1(B_2;\mathbb Z)=0$, $H^2(B_2;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z/2$, and $H^j(B_2;\mathbb Z)=0$ for every $j\ge3$: in degree one the map $\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z$ is injective multiplication by $2$, in degree two its cokernel is $\mathbb Z/2$ and the next relative group is zero, and in degree four the relative-to-absolute map is an isomorphism. In degree zero, the relative group vanishes, so $H^0(\mathbb{CP}^2;\mathbb Z)\to H^0(B_2;\mathbb Z)$ is an isomorphism; hence $B_2$ is connected. Repeat the relative calculation over $\mathbb Q$: the degree-two map is multiplication by $2$ and the degree-four map is the identity, both isomorphisms, so the pair sequence gives $H^j(B_2;\mathbb Q)=0$ for $j>0$ and $H^0(B_2;\mathbb Q)=\mathbb Q$. > Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the standard oriented $3$-sphere, choose its compact exterior $E_K$ with boundary torus $T_K$, and let $\mu$ and $\lambda$ be its positive meridian and preferred longitude. The exterior homology theorem gives $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z[\mu]$. Let $\phi:\pi_1(E_K)\to\mathbb Z$ be the composite of abelianization with the homomorphism $[\mu]\mapsto1$. For an integer $q\ge2$, let $\phi_q$ be the composite $\pi_1(E_K)\xrightarrow{\phi}\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z/q\mathbb Z$, and let $p_q:E_q\to E_K$ be the connected cover classified by $\ker\phi_q$. On $T_K$, the homomorphism sends $[\mu]\mapsto1$ and $[\lambda]\mapsto0$, so the preimage of $T_K$ is a connected torus cover whose fundamental group corresponds to $\langle\mu^q,\lambda\rangle$. Let $\widetilde\mu$ be the closed lift of $\mu^q$. Attach a solid torus to $E_q$ with its meridian identified with $\widetilde\mu$; the resulting oriented closed $3$-manifold is the $q$-fold cyclic branched cover $\Sigma_q(K)$. In tubular coordinates near $K$, the extended map to $S^3$ has local form $(s,w)\mapsto(s,w^q)$, and the deck group $\mathbb Z/q\mathbb Z$ acts by $w\mapsto e^{2\pi i/q}w$.

Let $M$ be the image of restriction $H^2(B;\mathbb Z)\to H^2(Y;\mathbb Z)$ and $M^\perp=\{x:\lambda_Y(m,x)=0\text{ for every }m\in M\}$. Then the boundary Spin$^c$ structures extending over $B$ form one affine coset of $M$, the pairing is nonsingular, $M=M^\perp$, and $|M|^2=|H_1(Y;\mathbb Z)|$.

Let $B$ be a smooth compact four-manifold with $H_*(B;\mathbb Q)\cong H_*(\mathrm{point};\mathbb Q)$ and oriented boundary the rational homology sphere $Y$, where $H_*(Y;\mathbb Q)\cong H_*(S^3;\mathbb Q)$. If a boundary Spin$^c$ structure $\mathfrak t$ extends over $B$, then its Heegaard Floer correction term vanishes: $d(Y,\mathfrak t)=0$. The extension hypothesis is essential; no vanishing is asserted for Spin$^c$ structures that do not extend.

Use the Ozsvath–Szabo orientation convention $L(p,1)$ given by positive $p$-surgery on the unknot and label its Spin$^c$ structures by $i\in\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z$, represented by $0\le i<p$. For every integer $p\ge1$,
$$d(L(p,1),i)=\frac{(2i-p)^2-p}{4p}.$$
For the opposite orientation the correction terms are negated, with the conjugate Spin$^c$ label understood.
